subject: Biology
title: Cell Theory: Three Rules of Life
description: A short lesson to help you apply Cell Theory: Three Rules of Life.

hook.text: Before the 1800s, people believed maggots sprang from meat and mice from grain.

buildup.text: Schleiden and Schwann proposed that all plants and animals are made of cells.

discovery.text: Virchow added the key third rule: every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.

twist.text: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment killed spontaneous generation for good.

climax.text: Three rules—all life is cells, cells are the basic unit, cells come from cells.

punchline.text: Three rules that explain all living things.

quiz.question: Who added the rule that all cells come from pre-existing cells?

details.summary: Cell theory states three foundational principles: all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Developed in the 1830s by Schleiden and Schwann, it remains the foundation of modern biology.
details.whyItMatters: Cell theory unified biology by establishing a universal framework for understanding life. Every discovery in genetics, medicine, and biotechnology builds on the principle that cells are the fundamental units of all living organisms.
takeaways: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells
The cell is the smallest unit that displays all properties of life
Every cell arises from the division of a pre-existing cell

faq.question: Who developed cell theory?
faq.answer: Matthias Schleiden proposed in 1838 that all plants are made of cells. Theodor Schwann extended this to animals in 1839. Rudolf Virchow added in 1855 that all cells come from pre-existing cells, completing the three tenets of cell theory.

faq.question: Are viruses an exception to cell theory?
faq.answer: Viruses are not made of cells and cannot reproduce independently, which is why most biologists do not consider them truly alive. They require host cells to replicate. This makes viruses a fascinating gray area at the boundary of life as defined by cell theory.
